knowledge_point.title: Finding the Value of an Unknown Such That a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of $k$ such that $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$, where

$$
\mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -4 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ k \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ exactly when $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2=\mathbf{b}$ has a solution. Equating coordinates gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}- 2 x_{1} - x_{2} &=8 \\ - 4 x_{1} + 2 x_{2} &=k \\ - 2 x_{1} + 2 x_{2} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Form the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & -1 & 8 \\ -4 & 2 & k \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{array}\right]
$$

Place the two known-coordinate equations first (a row permutation).

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-2 & -1 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1\leftarrow \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ -2 & 2 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow R_2-(-2)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 3 & -6 \\ -4 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-(-4)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 3 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & k - 16\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & k - 16\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-(4)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & k - 8\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row represents $0x_1+0x_2=k - 8$. Consistency therefore requires

$$
\begin{aligned}0 &=k - 8 \\ k &=8.\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot equations give $x_2=-2$ and $x_1=-3$. These values also establish sufficiency:

$$
(-3)\mathbf{a}_1+(-2)\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $k=8$ is the only value for which the vector lies in the span.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Value of an Unknown Such That a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of $k$ such that $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$, where

$$
\mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -15 \\ k\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ exactly when $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2=\mathbf{b}$ has a solution. Equating coordinates gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}- x_{1} - 3 x_{2} &=11 \\ 3 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} &=-15 \\ x_{1} + 2 x_{2} &=k\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Form the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 11 \\ 3 & 3 & -15 \\ 1 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1\leftarrow (-1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -11 \\ 3 & 3 & -15 \\ 1 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow R_2-(3)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -11 \\ 0 & -6 & 18 \\ 1 & 2 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-(1)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -11 \\ 0 & -6 & 18 \\ 0 & -1 & k + 11\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow \left(- \frac{1}{6}\right)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -11 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -1 & k + 11\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-(-1)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -11 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & k + 8\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row represents $0x_1+0x_2=k + 8$. Consistency therefore requires

$$
\begin{aligned}0 &=k + 8 \\ k &=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot equations give $x_2=-3$ and $x_1=-2$. These values also establish sufficiency:

$$
(-2)\mathbf{a}_1+(-3)\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -15 \\ -8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $k=-8$ is the only value for which the vector lies in the span.

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Value of an Unknown Such That a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
Find the value of $k$ such that $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$, where

$$
\mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ k \\ -15\end{bmatrix}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{b}\in\operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ exactly when $x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2=\mathbf{b}$ has a solution. Equating coordinates gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2 x_{1} + x_{2} &=3 \\ - 3 x_{1} + x_{2} &=k \\ - 3 x_{1} + 2 x_{2} &=-15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Form the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1 & k \\ -3 & 2 & -15\end{array}\right]
$$

Place the two known-coordinate equations first (a row permutation).

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 1 & 3 \\ -3 & 2 & -15 \\ -3 & 1 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_1\leftarrow \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ -3 & 2 & -15 \\ -3 & 1 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow R_2-(-3)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{7}{2} & - \frac{21}{2} \\ -3 & 1 & k\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-(-3)R_1$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{7}{2} & - \frac{21}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{5}{2} & k + \frac{9}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2\leftarrow \left(\frac{2}{7}\right)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{2} & k + \frac{9}{2}\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_3\leftarrow R_3-\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)R_2$.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & k + 12\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row represents $0x_1+0x_2=k + 12$. Consistency therefore requires

$$
\begin{aligned}0 &=k + 12 \\ k &=-12.\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot equations give $x_2=-3$ and $x_1=3$. These values also establish sufficiency:

$$
(3)\mathbf{a}_1+(-3)\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -12 \\ -15\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $k=-12$ is the only value for which the vector lies in the span.
